subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: lending to a friend without a plan [Pitfall]
passage: Last month I lent Ritu all my savings, two hundred rupees, for a craft kit. "I'll give it back soon, promise," said Ritu. Soon came and went. I did not want to ask, and Ritu did not seem to remember. After three weeks I finally said it, quietly. Ritu went red, said sorry, and paid back half the next week. Now if a friend asks, I lend a small amount, and we both say a date out loud. My sister Disha says that is being smart, not stingy. - Omar

qa.q: How much did Omar lend Ritu?
qa.a: Omar lent two hundred rupees.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling while waiting for Ritu to pay back?
qa.a: Awkward and uneasy, since Omar did not want to ask.

qa.q: What could Omar do next time a friend asks to borrow, and why?
qa.a: Omar could lend only a small amount and agree on a date, so a forgotten promise does not cost all the savings.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt when Omar finally asked?
qa.a: Embarrassed and sorry, since Ritu went red and paid back half the next week.

grounding: A child lends all the savings to a friend without a plan, waits weeks for repayment and learns to lend small with a date.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a packing and route list [Action]
passage: A week before the holidays, Sarita sat down with her mother Mehak and a blank sheet. "We're going to Nani's. What has to happen?" She wrote in a column: book tickets, pack clothes, food for the train, tell Nani the arrival time. Each item got a small box. Mummy booked the tickets that evening, and Sarita ticked her first box with a red pen. On Wednesday they packed together, on Thursday they made theplas, and the last box, call Nani, was ticked on Friday. On Saturday the train was on time, and there was nothing left to remember at the last minute.

qa.q: What items were on Sarita's list?
qa.a: The list had book tickets, pack clothes, food for the train and tell Nani the arrival time.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling as she ticked the last box?
qa.a: Satisfied and calm, since everything had been handled before the day.

qa.q: What other step could Sarita add to the list, and why?
qa.a: She could check the tickets and ID the day before, so a small mistake is found while there is still time.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Sarita's list?
qa.a: Mehak may find it helpful and be proud, since Sarita shares the planning and the ticking.

grounding: A girl breaks a visit to her grandparents into tasks, and ticks them off with her mother the week before.

subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]
passage: "Train, bus or car to Agra?" Papa asked at dinner. Wasim took a page and made three columns. Train: cheapest, a berth to sleep in, nobody has to drive tired at night. Bus: also cheap, but hours of bumps. Car: petrol and tolls add up, but we can stop for chai whenever we like. He gave each column stars for cost and comfort. "Train," he said. "The car is more fun, but the stops would cost extra and Papa would be tired." Mummy Rashmi read his page twice. "Let's book it."

qa.q: Which three ways of travelling did Wasim compare?
qa.a: He compared the train, the bus and the car.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as his family agreed to book the train?
qa.a: Proud and pleased, since his page helped them decide.

qa.q: What other factor could Wasim add to the comparison, and why?
qa.a: He could add the travel time and how much luggage each option allows, so the comparison is fair.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Wasim's page?
qa.a: Rashmi seems impressed, since she reads the page twice before saying let's book it.

grounding: A boy compares train, bus and car by cost and comfort, and helps the family choose the train.

subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]
passage: In their rented flat in Seville, Chidi announced his list: "Cathedral, palace, football stadium, river boat, the big park and the bullfight museum. Six places, two days!" He was already drawing a line on the tourist map. His father Emeka put a finger on the map, then pointed at the wall clock. "Chidi, the stadium is forty minutes away by bus. The palace queue can take an hour. Count with me." They wrote the hours on a page. Travel and queues filled the first day with three places at most. Chidi stared at the map. "It won't work, will it?" His sister Ines tapped the paper. "Pick three."

qa.q: How many places did Chidi want to visit?
qa.a: Chidi wanted to visit six places in two days.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when he saw the hours add up?
qa.a: Disappointed and surprised, since the travel and queues left room for only three places.

qa.q: What other approach could Chidi use to plan the days, and why?
qa.a: He could rank the places by how much he wants each and estimate the time each takes, so the top ones fit in first.

qa.q: How might Emeka see Chidi's long list?
qa.a: Emeka sees enthusiasm that is not yet realistic, so he does not say no and lets the map and clock show why.

grounding: A child wishes to see six places in two days until the father's map and the clock show travel time makes it impossible.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan to fit the budget [Revision]
passage: Note from Irfan, Amina's father. Friday: trip planning. I told Amina the family can spend ten thousand rupees. She spread her list on the table: fort, museum, water park, boat ride. She added up the costs from the printouts, saw that the water park alone took about a third of the money, and after a sigh crossed it out herself. "The fort and museum cost less and we all like them." She also suggested a picnic lunch. I only checked her sums. That evening I booked the fort and museum tickets, and Amina wrote the picnic on the list. - Irfan

qa.q: How much money can the family spend on the trip?
qa.a: The family can spend ten thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Amina feeling as she crossed out the water park?
qa.a: A little sad and disappointed, as her sigh shows, but sensible about the money.

qa.q: What could the family do if they still want the water park, and why?
qa.a: They could save it for a later trip or look for a cheaper day, so the wish is kept without breaking this budget.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Amina's change to the plan?
qa.a: Irfan sees a child who did the sums and decided herself, so he only checked and then booked the tickets.

grounding: A girl learns the family budget and removes the costly water park, keeping the fort and museum.

subtype: Approach: asking each family member for one wish [Action]
passage: Rukmini Ma'am's homework was to plan a trip that is fair to everybody. Chetan thought of the beach, his favourite. Then he wondered whether Dadi would like a beach. That evening he asked each person one question: "Which one place do you want most?" Dadi said the temple, Mummy the old bookshop, Papa the lighthouse, and his sister the aquarium. Next day in class he showed his chart: four places, each wish with a day beside it, and the beach on the way home as a fifth. "Nobody's wish is left out," he told Rukmini Ma'am, who pinned it on the display board.

qa.q: Which place did Dadi choose?
qa.a: Dadi chose the temple.

qa.q: What was Chetan thinking when he wondered whether Dadi would like a beach?
qa.a: He was thinking of others' tastes, and that a fair plan cannot rest on his own favourite alone.

qa.q: What could Chetan do if two wishes are far apart, and why?
qa.a: He could put them on different days, so nobody spends the whole day travelling between them.

qa.q: How might Chetan's sister feel seeing the aquarium on the chart?
qa.a: She is probably pleased and included, since her wish has a place and a day.

grounding: A boy asks each family member for one wish and builds the trip days around them so nobody feels ignored.

subtype: Approach: preparing for rain and delays [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. At the family planning table Trisha said, "Trains run late, and it might rain. What if we bring a plastic sheet, some snacks, and keep an indoor place like the museum as a back-up?" Papa Raghav wrote all three down.
Friday. The train was ninety minutes late. Nobody grumbled; everyone ate the snacks on the platform bench.
Saturday. Rain arrived after breakfast. They spread the sheet over the bags at the bus stop and went straight to the museum. "Trisha's plan just saved the day," said Papa.

qa.q: What three things did Trisha suggest carrying or having ready?
qa.a: She suggested a plastic sheet, some snacks and an indoor place like the museum as a back-up.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling on Saturday when the rain came?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased, since her plan for a wet day was ready.

qa.q: What else could Trisha add to prepare for delays, and why?
qa.a: She could add a buffer of extra time and a charged phone, so a late train does not spoil the connections.

qa.q: How does Papa Raghav see Trisha's suggestions?
qa.a: Papa Raghav takes them seriously, writing all three down, and later thanks her for saving the day.

grounding: A girl thinks ahead about a late train and rain, and suggests packing for a delay and a wet day.

subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage: Note from Charu, Kiran's mother. Two weeks before the holiday I asked Kiran what he would like to see. He shrugged, kept playing his game and said, "You decide." So the rest of us made the plan. On the second day, at the old stepwell, Kiran sat on a step and said it was boring; he wanted the model railway museum. It had never been on the list because he had never told us. He cried on the way to the next place, angry with us and, I think, a little with himself. That evening I asked him for one wish for the last day, and we changed the plan together. - Charu

qa.q: Where was Kiran when he said the day was boring?
qa.a: He was sitting on a step at the old stepwell.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on the way to the next place?
qa.a: Angry and upset, with the family and perhaps a little with himself.

qa.q: What could Kiran have done before the trip, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could have named one thing he wanted to see, so it could be included in the plan from the start.

qa.q: How does Charu see what went wrong on the trip?
qa.a: Charu notices that Kiran's wishes were missing rather than that the plan was bad, so she invites him to add one for the last day.

grounding: A child leaves the trip plan to adults, and is upset when the places do not match his interests.

subtype: Approach: drawing a map with a timetable [Action]
passage:
Monday. Seema drew the route to Jaipur on a sheet of paper, with three boxes for each day: morning, afternoon, evening. Fort, market and palace went into the boxes.
Tuesday. Papa Harish looked at it. Seema measured the distances on the map and wrote the travel times beside the arrows. "Fort to palace is forty minutes. My morning box is too full." She moved the market to the evening.
Saturday. On the trip the paper stayed in Papa's pocket, and at each stop Seema ticked a box. Nobody had to rush.

qa.q: What did Seema write beside the arrows?
qa.a: She wrote the travel times.

qa.q: What was Seema thinking on Tuesday when she measured the distances?
qa.a: She realised her morning box was too full and felt practical about fixing it, so she moved the market.

qa.q: What other approach could help Seema check the timings, and why?
qa.a: She could ask someone who has been there or look up a timetable, since a guess about travel time can be wrong.

qa.q: How might Papa Harish see Seema's paper plan?
qa.a: Papa Harish finds it useful, since he keeps it in his pocket for the whole trip.

grounding: A girl sketches the route with boxes for morning, afternoon and evening, and uses it to check the timings are realistic.

subtype: Approach: packing checklist based on past trips [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Joseph found last year's holiday photos and remembered the unhappy part: no charger for the phone, and Mummy's medicine box left on the shelf. They had searched three shops.
Tuesday. He took a fresh page and wrote the two things first, in capital letters: MEDICINE BOX, CHARGER. Then came shirts, snacks and towels.
Saturday. At the station, Papa Yogesh asked, "Did we forget anything?" Joseph unzipped the bag and showed the top of the list: both items ticked. Papa laughed. "You're our memory this time."

qa.q: What two things did Joseph write first?
qa.a: He wrote the medicine box and the charger.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he remembered last year's trip?
qa.a: Regretful and determined that the mistake would not happen again, remembering the search through three shops.

qa.q: What else could Joseph do to keep the list useful for future trips, and why?
qa.a: He could keep the list in a drawer and update it after each trip, so each trip's lessons are saved.

qa.q: How might Papa Yogesh see Joseph's list?
qa.a: Papa Yogesh is impressed and grateful, since he laughs and calls Joseph the family's memory.

grounding: A boy writes the items forgotten on a past trip at the top of his packing list, using earlier mistakes to prevent repeats.
